trace.reason: The first half of the claim is true: direct_tail picks the first row that fits the collateral rule, whoever's it is (lovejoin.rs:435-438). The consequence is false. The pick doesn't decide what goes into the box. direct_tail hands the tail's deposit every ADA-only row the evaluator accepts, as a single set of coins: the picked "collateral" plus every other such row as a payer (lovejoin.rs:441-446, 289-290). The session's own plain 5 ₳ always passes eval::refusal (eval.rs:62-70), so whenever it isn't the pick it is a payer. core's deposit spends every coin it is given (lovejoin/mod.rs:816-818), makes one 5 ₳ box from their total, and sends the rest back as change (803-812, 833). Ordering the rows either way gives the deposit the same input set, the same fee, the same 5 ₳ box and the same change. On chain the lead's scenario is the very transaction its own fix would build. The session's collateral is spent by the deposit in the same call, so nothing of it is left to mix later or to come back on its own. The return never sees it. What comes back directly is everything except one box's 5 ₳ and the fees, which is exactly privacy.md:429's "What it can't fix". The stranger's 5 ₳ just adds to that return. Nothing privacy.md says is hidden gets tied. Where the session's own 5 ₳ would be the only ADA-only row, it has no payer and the tail is refused (lovejoin.rs:447-449). In that case a stranger's 5 ₳ is what lets the collateral be mixed: the opposite of a downgrade (traced, not run). The order does matter in one way, and that is W1b's second point, not lead#1's. The tail's deposit change and mix change go to the first fitting row's address (lovejoin.rs:454-455, 474). A stranger's 5 ₳ at base(session payment key, stranger's stake key), listed first, puts both under the stranger's stake key until the return sweeps them. The run shows this. It puts no money at risk: the session key spends it and the sweep takes it. It costs the user no rewards, since the session's stake key is never registered. It adds no new link, because every return already spends that stranger row under the session's key. So it's low at most: a check the chain path has (lovejoin.rs:1057-1065) and direct_tail lacks, with nothing reachable today. Lead#1 as described has no harm.

trace.fix_notes: Lead#1 needs no fix. Its proposed fix ("take the funding's recorded 5 ₳ for the tail") builds the same deposit in the lead's scenario: the same inputs, fee, box and change, as the test asserts. It isn't worth adding for privacy. W1b's second point is the one real consequence of the pick, and it is separate from lead#1. With a stranger's 5 ₳ at base(session payment key, stranger's stake key) listed first, direct_tail sends the tail's deposit change and its mix change to that address (lovejoin.rs:454-455, 474). The test prints this as true for both. They stay there until the return sweeps them, which can be longer if the mix has to be resumed: collateral_mix then pays from the largest such row and sends its change to `payer.address` (lovejoin.rs:539-548). It's harmless today: the session key spends it, nothing the user owns is lost, and it adds no new link. It is inconsistent with the chain path's rule, "never first a stranger's" (lovejoin.rs:1057-1065). If the lead wants it closed, the class fix is to choose the change address the way Holdings does: the session's own transactions' row first (`own`, which session_return already has), or the worker's chosen collateral passed as an OutRef, as holdings_of takes one. The worker's chain path already prefers the funding's 5 ₳ (sessions.ts:4625). W1b notes a third rule for the same pick, session_collateral (lib.rs:985), which admits 5 ₳ rows carrying a datum that fits_collateral refuses. Such a fix adds no refusal and changes no privacy default, so it isn't an owner call. Grade it low at most, as a check missing with no reachable harm. impact.reason:
The lead's harm doesn't happen. It says the session's own collateral comes back unmixed when a stranger's 5 ₳ is labelled the collateral. But in `direct_tail` the label decides nothing about what gets spent. Any other UTxO that fits the collateral rule also passes the payer filters, so the session's own 5 ₳ becomes a payer. The deposit then spends every coin as an input, and Pallas sorts the inputs. Either way it is the same deposit: the same inputs, one 5 ₳ box, the same change and the same amount swept back. Value inside one transaction has no identity, so nobody on chain can say the box "is" the stranger's 5 ₳. Nothing of the session's own collateral is left to come back unmixed, then or later. privacy.md promises one 5 ₳ box mixed instead of brought back "under the session's history", and a deposit and mix "tied to it as any chain's are"; both still hold.

A stranger can get listed first: rows are ordered by tx_hash, so a lower hash comes first, by chance or by grinding. But being first only changes one thing: the deposit's and the mix's change go to that row's address. A stranger can pick the stake part of an address that carries the session's payment key. So the session's in-flight change can sit under the stranger's stake credential, from the deposit until the sweep. No money is lost: the session key still spends it and the sweep brings it back. No rewards are lost: the session's own stake key is never registered. No new link appears: in either labelling the deposit spends the stranger's UTxO at that address. This does go against the rule `holdings_of` states for the chain path (never send change first to a stranger's address). It is harmless today, so it stays a nit, not a finding.
impact.evidence:
1. The pick: `seedelf-platform/seedelf-web-wallet/wasm/src/lovejoin.rs:435-438`, `let collateral = utxos.iter().find(|u| fits_collateral(u))`. Its caller passes every row at the account unfiltered (`lib.rs:1425`, `&request.utxos`).
2. The payers: `lovejoin.rs:441-446` keeps every other ADA-only row that `seedelf_core::eval::refusal` passes. `refusal` (`seedelf-core/src/eval.rs:62-70`) refuses only a reference script or an unreadable inline datum. `fits_collateral` (`lovejoin.rs:348-354`) already forbids both. So when the stranger's 5 ₳ is labelled the collateral, the session's own 5 ₳ is a payer, and the reverse holds too.
3. One deposit takes them all: `CollateralTail::build` sets `coins = [collateral] + payers` (`lovejoin.rs:289-290`) and calls core's `collateral_tail` (`seedelf-core/src/lovejoin/mod.rs:2418`), which calls `deposit`, then `deposit_across`. That adds every input: `mod.rs:816`, `for held in inputs { tx = tx.input(held.input()); }`. It makes one 5 ₳ box, with change of total − 5 ₳ − fee. `build_conway_raw` sorts inputs (`pallas-txbuilder-0.35.1/src/conway.rs:47`, `sort_unstable_by_key(|x| (x.transaction_id, x.index))`), so the input list is the same bytes in either labelling.
4. The rest is the same set too: `spent` = the collateral plus the payers, and `rest = [mix change] + the untouched rows` (`lovejoin.rs:466-475`). The returned figure is identical.
5. Already pinned: `wasm/tests/lovejoin_test.rs:1793-1829` asserts that the return takes only the mix's change (`result.inputs == 1`). So the deposit took both the 20 ₳ and the 5 ₳. That test has no case with two 5 ₳ rows.
6. Ordering: `extension/src/background/koios.ts:1331` lists rows by `order=tx_hash.asc,tx_index.asc`, and `data-layer.ts:244` goes through the same client. A stranger's row comes first whenever its hash sorts lower: reachable, but it changes nothing in steps 3–4.
7. The one real difference: `lovejoin.rs:454` and `:474` take the change address from `collateral.address`. `payment_key_of` (`lib.rs:286-299`) accepts any Shelley address with the session's payment key, whatever its stake part. The session's own address is base(0/i, 2/i), and 2/i is never registered (`docs/keys-and-accounts.md:77`).
   - The chain path's rule says otherwise: `lovejoin.rs:1057-1058`, "never first a stranger's, which may name the session's key under a stake key of its own" (commit 62162483).
   - Nothing reads that address: `crossCheck` (`lovejoin.ts:4805`) measures scripts only, and the review's figures come from WebAssembly's numbers (`sessions.ts:4803-4820`).
8. Since 24c5c62a (2026-10-23), first in `web-wallet/1.6.0`.

impact.fix_notes:
The lead's fix as written would cost privacy. "Only the funding's 5 ₳ output" would stop the tail from mixing a top-up's new 5 ₳ collateral (privacy.md:458), and the 5 ₳ that L20 and §2.15 accept as a fallback. Those would then come back directly.

If the owner wants the two paths to agree (optional hardening, no harm today):
- In `direct_tail`, prefer a fitting row whose tx_hash is in `own` before any other fitting row (`own` already reaches `session_return`).
- Take the change address as `holdings_of` does: an own row's address, never first a stranger's.
- Fix the comments that call any fitting 5 ₳ "the session's own": `fits_collateral`'s doc, `DirectTail`'s, `direct_tail`'s, and `CollateralTail::build`'s error text.

The family has the same harmless shape: the worker's chain fallback (`sessions.ts:4625`) and the merged return's `session_collateral` (`lib.rs:985`). In each, the 5 ₳ not picked is spent in the same transaction or chain. In the chain path the change also follows the collateral's address (`lovejoin.rs:1059`), so a stranger's fallback 5 ₳ takes it there too, but only once the funding's collateral is gone.

A test for the trace verifier: rows of the stranger's 5 ₳ (hash sorted first), the session's own 5 ₳ and a 20 ₳ row. Assert that the deposit spends all three in both orders and that `result.inputs == 1`. Assert which address the change output goes to; that shows the leftover difference.
